narrationScript: Now, let's dive into a fundamental concept: the Document Object Model, or DOM. Think of the DOM as a programming interface for HTML and XML documents. When your browser loads an HTML page, it doesn't just display text; it parses that HTML and creates a live, tree-like representation of its entire structure. Every HTML element, every attribute, even text itself, becomes an object within this tree. This is where JavaScript becomes incredibly powerful, because it can interact directly with this DOM. It allows you to dynamically read, modify, add, or even delete elements and their content or styles on the fly. A common way to select a specific element in the DOM is using `document.getElementById()`, targeting an element by its unique ID attribute. Once you have a reference to an element, you can manipulate its properties. For instance, `element.textContent` allows you to change the visible text, and `element.style.color` lets you directly modify its CSS style. A common mistake here is trying to access DOM elements before they've been fully loaded by the browser, which is why script placement, as we discussed, is so important.
deliveryNotes: Explain DOM as a 'live, tree-like representation'
